Common Tangent Sangaku

GeometryCirclesTriangles
Game: Two circles sit inside an angle, each touching both sides, and the small circle also touches a chord across the big one.
How to play: Drag the dots C, O and Q, or focus a dot and use the arrow keys. Q slides along the line from C to O; switch on the names, statement or hint to see more.
Look for the math

Move the three points and the two circles change size, yet they keep three special contacts at once. This old temple problem asks why those contacts always come together.

Three contacts in one picture

Let the angle have vertex C and let the two circles be centred at O (the big one) and Q (the small one). Both touch the angle's two sides, so their centres lie on the bisector of the angle. Cut the big circle with the chord MN perpendicular to OC. The page's claim is that any two of these force the third: (1) M and N are where the big circle touches the sides; (2) the small circle is tangent to MN; (3) Q lies on the big circle.

The exact radius rule

Write d = CO and t = CQ/d. The applet keeps Q on the segment CO, so the big radius is R = OQ = (1 − t)d. The small circle's radius is

r = R × CQ / CO = R(1 − R/d) = d × t(1 − t)

At the applet's starting value t = 0.6 this gives R = 0.4d and r = 0.24d. The chord MN is cut at distance √(d² − R²) from C; that is exactly where the big circle's radius meets each side at a right angle, so condition 1 holds.

Why two conditions force the third

Let s = sin(α) = R/d for half the angle. A circle touching both sides with centre x from C has radius xs. The tangency chord sits at d − Rs from C, and the small circle touching it from the C side needs xs = (d − Rs) − x; hence x = d − R, exactly the near point where the small centre lies on the big circle. The same equation read backwards gives the other two implications. The logic test checks all three pairs independently on a grid of 17 angles and 6 distances, and re-measures every contact from the resulting points.

What this port keeps, and what it changes

The page treats only the case where O is farther from C than Q; the applet also keeps Q between C and O, so this port does too. It also keeps the applet's guard that refuses a diagram with CQ < 2, and its Show names, Show statement and Show hint options. The drawing is modern SVG instead of AWT, and a Reset button returns to the opening picture; neither changes the geometry. The logic test compares the geometry with a second transcription of the applet's own Compute() over hundreds of configurations.

Try dragging Q to the midpoint of CO: the small circle is then as large as it can get. Switch on the hint to see the tangent line at the far point V and the larger triangle around the big circle.
